### Create a rule

A **rule** captures one expectation about your data — "this column is never blank", "an amount is never negative", "a status is one of a known set". You write it once in the **Rules Registry** and reuse it on as many tables as you like.

This page walks through creating a rule the no-code way. It's the most common thing you'll do in DQX Studio, so it's worth reading once end to end.

Before you start

You need the **Rule Author** role (or higher) to create rules. If you only see a read-only view, ask your admin — see [Roles & permissions](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/permissions-and-entitlements.md).

#### Start a new rule[​](#start-a-new-rule "Direct link to Start a new rule")

Open **Rules** in the sidebar and click **New rule**. The rule editor opens on the **About** tab, where you describe what the rule is. You'll fill in the *details* here, and the *logic* on the Implementation tab next.

Fill in:

* **Name** — a short, human readable name. Say what good looks like, not what's wrong: *"Email is present"*, not *"email null check"*.
* **Description** — one line on what the rule checks and why it matters.
* **Default severity** — how much a failure of this rule matters: [**Low**, **Medium**, **High**, or **Critical**](/dqx/docs/studio.md#severity) (your organization can customize these levels). Severity is a priority for triage and reporting, not a pass/fail switch — it's the starting point, and you can override it for a specific table when you apply the rule.
* **Dimension** — which [aspect of quality](/dqx/docs/studio.md#quality-dimensions) this measures (completeness, validity, accuracy, and so on). This is what lets you later report quality *by category*.
* **Tags** *(optional)* — labels for organizing and filtering rules. Some tags are [governed tags](#governed-tags) that make a rule apply automatically wherever that kind of data appears.

##### Governed tags: apply a rule automatically[​](#governed-tags "Direct link to Governed tags: apply a rule automatically")

A **governed tag** is a label your organization agrees on for a *kind* of data — `pii`, `region`, `class.location`, and so on. Governed tags are defined in **Unity Catalog**, not in DQX Studio, and are the shared vocabulary you already use to classify columns.

Instead of pointing a rule at a named column, you can point one of its columns at a **tag**: on the column, click **+ Apply to a tag** and pick from the searchable list of Unity Catalog tags. The rule then **auto-applies** to any table column carrying that tag — a rule scoped to `pii` lands on every `pii` column across your tables, and picks up new ones the moment they're tagged. No hunting down an `email` column that's called `email_address` on one table and `contact_email` on another.

Checks that arrive this way are marked with a **matched-tag chip** on the table's [Apply Rules tab](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md), so you can tell they came from a governed tag rather than being mapped by hand.

Governed tags vs. rule labels

Governed tags attach to a **column** inside a rule and drive auto-apply. They're different from the plain **Tags** field above, which just helps you organize and find rules. Admins manage the organization's tags under [Governance](/dqx/docs/studio/governance.md).

#### Define what the rule checks[​](#define-what-the-rule-checks "Direct link to Define what the rule checks")

Switch to the **Implementation** tab. This is where you say *what* makes data pass or fail — without writing code.

##### Columns are placeholders, not real columns[​](#columns-are-placeholders-not-real-columns "Direct link to Columns are placeholders, not real columns")

Notice the column is written as `{{column_1}}` — a **placeholder**. Because a rule lives in the Registry and is meant to be *reused*, you don't pick a real column here. You choose the actual column later, when you [apply the rule to a table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md). That's how one "is never blank" rule can protect `email` on one table and `phone` on another.

##### A rule can use more than one column[​](#a-rule-can-use-more-than-one-column "Direct link to A rule can use more than one column")

A rule isn't limited to a single column. Under **Columns used** you can add several placeholders — `{{column_1}}`, `{{column_2}}`, and so on — and your condition can reference all of them. This is what lets a rule express a relationship *between* columns, not just a fact about one. For example:

* **A date ordering:** `{{end_date}}` is on or after `{{start_date}}`.
* **Conditional presence:** if `{{payment_method}}` is `card`, then `{{card_last_four}}` must not be blank.
* **A combined uniqueness key:** the pair `{{customer_id}}` + `{{order_date}}` never appears twice.
* **A cross-column comparison:** `{{discounted_price}}` is not greater than `{{list_price}}`.

Just as with a single-column rule, you map each placeholder to a real column when you apply the rule to a table — so a multi-column rule stays just as reusable.

Under **Condition**, you build a simple sentence: *IF `{{column_1}}` …* and then pick what must be true. There are three ways to express what makes data pass or fail, from the simplest to the most powerful. Most rules only ever need the first.

Not sure which check you want?

Describe it in plain English instead — the **Generate** box at the top of the editor drafts a check for you. See [Generate a rule with AI](#generate-a-rule-with-ai) below.

##### Simple checks[​](#simple-checks "Direct link to Simple checks")

The no-code option: pick a ready-made check from a catalog, fill in a couple of values, and you're done. It covers most of what you'll want to check.

![Choosing a ready-made check from the catalog of built-in checks](/dqx/img/studio/create_rule_basic_checks_light.png)![Choosing a ready-made check from the catalog of built-in checks](/dqx/img/studio/create_rule_basic_checks_dark.png)

When you open the picker you'll see the built-in checks, grouped and searchable. You don't need to memorize them — but here's what's available, by what you're trying to verify:

| You want to check that…                                                      | Checks to reach for                                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **A value is present** (never blank)                                         | is not null; is not null and not empty                                                                               |
| **A value is in an allowed set**                                             | is in list; is not in list                                                                                           |
| **A number or date is in range**                                             | is in range; is not less than / is not greater than; is not negative                                                 |
| **A value matches a format** (email, phone, an ID shaped like `NNN-NN-NNNN`) | matches a pattern; is a valid date / timestamp                                                                       |
| **There are no unwanted duplicates**                                         | is unique — across one column *or several columns combined*                                                          |
| **Dates make sense for "now"**                                               | a timestamp is not in the future; a date is recent enough                                                            |
| **A group of rows as a whole behaves**                                       | aggregate checks (an average / sum / count stays within bounds, overall or per group); rolling-window outlier checks |
| **Data lines up with another table**                                         | a value must exist in a reference table (foreign-key style); the table's shape matches an expected schema            |

Patterns without the jargon

A "pattern" (regular expression) is just a way to describe the *shape* of text — for example "three digits, a dash, two digits, a dash, four digits" for a Social Security number. You describe the shape; you don't need to be an expert.

For the exact, function-by-function reference — every built-in check, its precise behavior, and the arguments it accepts — see the [Quality checks reference](/dqx/docs/reference/quality_checks.md) in DQX Core.

##### Condition builder[​](#condition-builder "Direct link to Condition builder")

The condition builder lets you **chain several checks together with `AND` and `OR`** to express real-world rules that a single check can't. You build each step the same visual way, then combine them.

For example:

* *`{{email}}` is not blank **AND** matches an email pattern.*
* *`{{status}}` is `shipped` **OR** `{{status}}` is `delivered`.*
* *`{{discount}}` is between 0 and 100 **AND** `{{amount}}` is not negative.*
* *If `{{payment_method}}` is `card`, **then** `{{card_last_four}}` is present **AND** is four digits.*

Because a condition built this way can reference [more than one column](#a-rule-can-use-more-than-one-column) and combine several tests, it's the way to capture nuanced expectations without dropping into SQL.

The condition builder also has an **Advanced** box for the less common cases. Expand it when your rule needs more than a plain condition:

* **Filter** — apply the rule to only *some* rows. A filter is a condition that decides which rows the check runs on, so you can say "only check `amount` on rows where `status` is `active`" or "only rows from this year". Rows that don't match the filter are skipped rather than failed.
* **Join / reference another table** — check a value against a *different* table. This is how referential checks work — for example "every `product_id` in orders must exist in the products table". You point at the reference table and the columns to match on, and DQX Studio compares against it when the rule runs. See [Cross-table rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/cross-table-rules.md) for the full picture (built-in check, visual join, and SQL).

Most rules never need the Advanced box — reach for it when a rule has to target a subset of rows or look something up in another table.

##### Custom SQL[​](#custom-sql "Direct link to Custom SQL")

For advanced users: when even the condition builder can't express what you need, choose **SQL** under Custom condition. You can write either:

* a **plain condition** over placeholders (always [row-level](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/row-and-dataset-level.md)), or
* a **full query** (`SELECT … FROM {{input_view}} …`), where you set **Applies to** to **Row-level** or **Dataset-level**.

This is also the path for complex [cross-table](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/cross-table-rules.md) comparisons. The query must be a single read-only `SELECT` — DQX Studio rejects anything that writes or runs multiple statements.

#### Cross-table rules[​](#cross-table-rules "Direct link to Cross-table rules")

Some checks span two (or more) tables — for example "every order points at a real customer", or "a line item's price matches the catalogue".

There are three ways to write one:

* **A built-in referential check** — "value exists in a reference table" (foreign-key style). Best for the common case.
* **The visual builder's Advanced → Joins** — when the lookup is part of a larger condition.
* **Custom SQL** — for comparisons or aggregates the builder can't express. Read the monitored table with `FROM {{input_view}}`, name joined tables with a fully qualified `catalog.schema.table`, and (for a full query) return a boolean `condition` column where `TRUE` means fail. You can also write a boolean expression followed by `JOIN` clauses and let Studio wrap it.

Step-by-step examples (including row-level vs dataset-level SQL, permissions, and common pitfalls) live on [Cross-table rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/cross-table-rules.md). For when to use **Row-level** vs **Dataset-level**, see [Row-level vs dataset-level rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/row-and-dataset-level.md).

#### Generate a rule with AI[​](#generate-a-rule-with-ai "Direct link to Generate a rule with AI")

If you'd rather describe what you want than build it by hand, use the **Generate** box at the top of the editor. Type the expectation in plain English and DQX Studio proposes a matching check with its settings filled in. Good prompts are specific:

* `order amount must be positive and under $1,000,000`
* `email should look like a valid email address`
* `status must be one of placed, shipped, delivered, cancelled`
* `signup date can't be in the future`
* `card last four must be present when payment method is card`

The app reads your description, picks a matching rule (or chains a few together), and fills in the details — the allowed values, the range, the pattern, and so on.

You can also ask for a specific *type* of rule rather than only describing the data expectation. Say you want a uniqueness check, a range check, or a pattern/regex check, and the assistant builds that kind of rule — for example `make a uniqueness check on customer id` or `add a regex check for a UK postcode`.

Always review AI output

A generated rule is a **starting point**, not a finished rule. Read what the app proposed, adjust anything that isn't quite right, and run the **Test** tab before saving — AI can misread a description or pick settings you didn't intend. Once saved, a generated rule follows the same review, approval, and audit path as any other rule.

#### Test it before you save[​](#test-it-before-you-save "Direct link to Test it before you save")

Open the **Test** tab to try the rule against a small sample of real data before you commit to it. A test run shows how many rows would pass or fail, and lets you see example rows that don't pass — so you can confirm the rule does what you meant.

Testing changes nothing: it reads a sample, evaluates the rule, and persists nothing. It's the safest way to catch a rule that's too strict or too loose before it goes live.

You don't have to hand-write test cases either. DQX Studio can generate tests for you with AI — it looks at what the rule checks and produces example rows that should pass and fail, so you can confirm the rule behaves the way you meant without inventing sample data yourself.

#### Save and submit[​](#save-and-submit "Direct link to Save and submit")

When you're happy:

* **Save as draft** keeps the rule private to you while you keep working on it.
* **Save & submit** sends it for review. An approver checks it and, once approved, the rule becomes active and available to apply to tables.

Why can't I just make it live myself?

Unless you're an approver or admin, you can't approve your own rule. This "four-eyes" step means someone other than the author signs off before a rule affects any run — a simple guardrail against mistakes. See the [Approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md).

#### What happens next[​](#what-happens-next "Direct link to What happens next")

An approved rule sits in the Registry, ready to use. It doesn't check anything on its own yet — the next step is to [apply it to a table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md), which turns your reusable rule into a live check.

#### Other ways to create rules[​](#other-ways-to-create-rules "Direct link to Other ways to create rules")

You can also [import rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/import-rules.md) you already have, from DQX YAML or an Open Data Contract. And if you're not sure what to check yet, [profiling](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/profiling.md) scans a table and suggests candidate rules from the data.


---

### Cross-table rules

A **cross-table rule** checks that data in one table is consistent with data in another — for example "every order points at a real customer", or "a line item's price matches the product catalogue".

You still author the rule once in the [Rules Registry](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md) and [apply it to a monitored table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md). The monitored table is the one being checked; the other table is a **reference** (joined or looked up) while the rule runs.

There are three ways to write a cross-table rule. Start with the simplest that covers your case.

#### Pick the right approach[​](#pick-the-right-approach "Direct link to Pick the right approach")

| What you need                                                                                            | Use                                            |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Every value in a column must exist in another table (foreign-key style)                                  | A **built-in referential check**               |
| A condition that also looks up another table (for example "status is active **and** the product exists") | The **visual builder** with a join in Advanced |
| A comparison, aggregate, or multi-table query the builder can't express                                  | **Custom SQL**                                 |

New to rule authoring?

Start with [Create a rule](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md) for the overall flow (About → Implementation → Test → Save). This page only covers the cross-table parts of Implementation.

#### Built-in referential check[​](#built-in-referential-check "Direct link to Built-in referential check")

For the common case — "every `product_id` in orders exists in products":

1. Open **Rules** → **New rule**, fill in the About tab, then go to **Implementation**.
2. Under **Condition**, open the check picker and choose the built-in check that requires a value to **exist in a reference table** (foreign-key style).
3. Point it at the **reference table** and the columns to match on.
4. Test, save, and apply the rule to the monitored table as usual.

This is the no-code path. Prefer it whenever a simple "must exist over there" expectation is enough — it is faster to author and usually cheaper to run than an equivalent join in SQL.

#### Visual builder with a join[​](#visual-builder-with-a-join "Direct link to Visual builder with a join")

Use this when the cross-table lookup is part of a larger condition — for example chaining several checks with `AND` / `OR`, or filtering which rows to evaluate.

1. In **Condition**, choose **Custom condition** (or start from the visual builder after picking Custom condition).
2. Build the main condition as usual with column placeholders such as `{{product_id}}`.
3. Open **Advanced** → **Joins**, click **Add join**, and pick the reference table (catalog → schema → table).
4. Set the join keys (which column on the monitored table matches which column on the joined table).
5. Use the joined columns in your condition where needed.

When you apply the rule later, you only map the monitored table's placeholders to real columns. The joined table is already named in the rule.

Joins keep the rule row-level

Adding a join in the builder does **not** turn the rule into a single table-wide verdict. Results are still matched back to individual rows using the join keys. See [Row-level vs dataset-level rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/row-and-dataset-level.md).

#### Custom SQL[​](#custom-sql "Direct link to Custom SQL")

Choose **SQL** from the check picker (under **Custom condition**) when you need full control — for example a price comparison across tables, or an aggregate that spans a join.

##### How to reference tables and columns[​](#how-to-reference-tables-and-columns "Direct link to How to reference tables and columns")

* **The table being checked** — in a full SQL query, read it with `FROM {{input_view}}`. That placeholder becomes the monitored table when the rule runs (you don't hard-code its name in the rule).
* **Columns of the monitored table** — reusable placeholders such as `{{customer_id}}` or `{{unit_price}}`. You map those when you apply the rule.
* **Joined / reference tables** — use a **fully qualified name** (`catalog.schema.table`). Write that name in the SQL, or declare the join in **Advanced → Joins**.

You can either declare the join in **Advanced → Joins** *or* write the `JOIN` yourself in the SQL editor — **not both**. Declaring the same join twice produces invalid SQL.

##### Two shapes of SQL[​](#two-shapes-of-sql "Direct link to Two shapes of SQL")

Studio accepts either:

1. **A boolean expression, optionally followed by `JOIN` clauses** — the expression is TRUE when the row is **valid**. Studio wraps it into a query for you (inverting it into a `condition` column that marks failures).
2. **A full `SELECT`** — you own the query. It must return a boolean column named `condition`, where **`condition` is TRUE when the check fails**.

Both shapes are single read-only statements. DQX Studio rejects anything that writes data or runs multiple statements.

##### Row-level SQL — predicate + join (simplest)[​](#row-level-sql--predicate--join-simplest "Direct link to Row-level SQL — predicate + join (simplest)")

Write the **passing** case as a boolean expression, then append the join. Set **Applies to** to **Row-level** and choose the key columns to **merge results back on**.

```sql
-- Orphaned orders: customer_id must match a real customer
{{customer_id}} IS NOT NULL AND c.id IS NOT NULL
LEFT JOIN catalog.schema.customers c ON c.id = {{customer_id}}

```

```sql
-- Line item priced the same as the product catalogue
{{unit_price}} = p.list_price
JOIN catalog.schema.products p ON p.id = {{product_id}}

```

Studio turns that into a `SELECT … AS condition FROM {{input_view}} …` under the hood, projecting your merge keys so failures can be attributed to individual rows.

##### Row-level SQL — full query[​](#row-level-sql--full-query "Direct link to Row-level SQL — full query")

When you need aggregates per key, filters, or more control, write the full `SELECT` yourself. Include every **merge column** in the select list, plus a boolean `condition` column (`TRUE` = fail). Set the merge columns in **Advanced → Merge results back on** as column slots like `{{order_id}}`, which Studio maps to the table's real columns.

```sql
-- Orphaned orders, written as a full query
SELECT
  o.{{order_id}},
  o.{{customer_id}},
  (c.id IS NULL) AS condition
FROM {{input_view}} o
LEFT JOIN catalog.schema.customers c ON o.{{customer_id}} = c.id

```

```sql
-- Line item priced differently from the product catalogue
SELECT
  i.{{order_item_id}},
  i.{{product_id}},
  (i.{{unit_price}} <> p.list_price) AS condition
FROM {{input_view}} i
JOIN catalog.schema.products p ON i.{{product_id}} = p.id

```

##### Dataset-level SQL[​](#dataset-level-sql "Direct link to Dataset-level SQL")

One verdict for the whole dataset. Set **Applies to** to **Dataset-level**. The query must aggregate to **exactly one row** and return a boolean `condition` (`TRUE` = fail).

```sql
-- Fail the whole table if any order has no matching customer
SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 AS condition
FROM {{input_view}} o
LEFT JOIN catalog.schema.customers c ON o.{{customer_id}} = c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL

```

```sql
-- Fail if more than 1% of line items disagree with the catalogue price
SELECT
  (SUM(CASE WHEN i.{{unit_price}} <> p.list_price THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
    * 1.0 / COUNT(*)) > 0.01 AS condition
FROM {{input_view}} i
JOIN catalog.schema.products p ON i.{{product_id}} = p.id

```

Match the switch to the query

**Row-level** without merge keys, or **Dataset-level** without a single aggregated row, fails when the rule runs. The editor warns about these cases — don't ignore those messages. For more on when to pick each level, see [Row-level vs dataset-level rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/row-and-dataset-level.md).

##### Write or improve SQL with AI[​](#write-or-improve-sql-with-ai "Direct link to Write or improve SQL with AI")

In the SQL editor, use **Write with AI** / **Improve** to draft a cross-table predicate from a plain-English description. Mention:

* the **fully qualified** reference table (`catalog.schema.table`)
* whether the check should be **row-level** or **dataset-level** (the **Applies to** toggle is sent to the model as context)

Always review the generated SQL and run **Test** before saving.

#### Permissions you need[​](#permissions-you-need "Direct link to Permissions you need")

Cross-table rules read more than the monitored table:

* **You** need `SELECT` on the monitored table *and* every reference table you join (authoring and testing run as you).
* The **app identity** that runs scheduled checks also needs `SELECT` on those reference tables, or scheduled runs will fail even when your interactive test passed.

If a table isn't offered in the join picker, it's a Unity Catalog permissions question — see [Permissions & entitlements](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/permissions-and-entitlements.md).

#### Common pitfalls[​](#common-pitfalls "Direct link to Common pitfalls")

| Symptom                                                                  | Likely cause                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "Declare the join in the card below or write it in the query — not both" | The same join is declared in **Advanced → Joins** *and* typed in the SQL. Pick one.                                                   |
| Query uses columns of the table being checked but never reads it         | A full `SELECT` forgot `FROM {{input_view}}`.                                                                                         |
| Rule fails at runtime with a single-row / merge error                    | **Applies to** doesn't match the query shape (row-level needs merge keys in the `SELECT`; dataset-level must return exactly one row). |
| Test works, scheduled run fails                                          | The schedule runs as the app identity, which may lack `SELECT` on the reference table.                                                |
| Unexpected failures after a join                                         | Remember: in a full `SELECT`, `condition` is TRUE when the check **fails**. Don't invert it by accident.                              |

#### After you save[​](#after-you-save "Direct link to After you save")

Cross-table rules follow the same path as any other rule: test on sample data, save as draft or submit for approval, then [apply the rule](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md) to the monitored table. To understand how row-level vs dataset-level choices show up in results, see [Row-level vs dataset-level rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/row-and-dataset-level.md).


---

### Row-level vs dataset-level rules

Every rule answers one of two questions:

* **Row-level** — *Does this individual row look good?* Failures are attributed to specific rows (and you can open sample failing records).
* **Dataset-level** — *Does a group of rows look good together?* The check is evaluated over a set of rows — the whole dataset, or groups of rows within it — rather than each row on its own. The failure is still recorded on the offending rows: checks that can single out the culprits mark exactly those rows (for example duplicate keys, or rows missing a reference), while checks whose verdict is about the group as a whole (a global aggregate, a schema check) mark every row in the failing group.

Most rules are row-level. Reach for dataset-level when the expectation is about the whole table or a *set* of rows rather than one row on its own — for example "the table is not empty", "the average order amount stays in bounds per region", or "there are no orphaned orders".

Why this matters for results

A row-level failure points you straight at the bad records. A dataset-level failure is recorded on rows too: some checks pinpoint the specific offenders (duplicates, referential gaps), while others flag every row in the failing group (a global aggregate, a schema check). Choose based on how you want to investigate later — see [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md).

#### How authoring decides the level[​](#how-authoring-decides-the-level "Direct link to How authoring decides the level")

You don't always pick this yourself. It depends on how you write the rule.

| How you author            | Who decides row vs dataset  | What to know                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Built-in check**        | The check — fixed           | Some checks always evaluate each row (for example "is not null"). Others evaluate a group of rows (uniqueness, some aggregates, reference lookups) and still attribute failures to individual rows when they can identify them. |
| **Visual builder**        | Derived from what you build | A plain condition is row-level. Adding **joins** or **grouping** still keeps the rule row-level: results are merged back onto key columns.                                                                                      |
| **SQL — plain condition** | Always row-level            | A boolean expression over `{{column}}` placeholders is evaluated per row. There is no **Applies to** switch.                                                                                                                    |
| **SQL — full query**      | **You choose**              | The Condition header shows **Applies to**: **Row-level** or **Dataset-level**.                                                                                                                                                  |

#### Built-in checks[​](#built-in-checks "Direct link to Built-in checks")

When you pick a ready-made check, its level is a property of that check — not a setting you change.

Examples (not an exhaustive list):

* **Typically row-level:** is not null; is in list; is in range; matches a pattern; date/timestamp checks.
* **Evaluated over a group of rows:** is unique; some aggregate / rolling checks; looking a value up in a reference table.

Even when a check evaluates a group of rows to *compute* its result, the failure is always recorded on the offending rows — this is core DQX behaviour. Checks that can single out the culprits mark exactly those rows (for example duplicate keys, or values missing from a reference table); checks whose verdict is about the group as a whole (a global aggregate, a schema check) mark every row in the failing group.

#### Visual builder[​](#visual-builder "Direct link to Visual builder")

In the visual builder:

1. Build your `IF …` conditions as usual.
2. Optionally open **Advanced** for a **filter**, **joins**, or **group-by**.

Joins and grouping do **not** flip the rule to a single group-wide verdict. They stay row-level: DQX merges results back using the join / group keys so each failing row can still be found.

For a true "one verdict for the whole dataset" custom rule, use a [SQL query](#sql-full-query) set to **Dataset-level**.

#### SQL — plain condition[​](#sql--plain-condition "Direct link to SQL — plain condition")

If your SQL is a boolean expression (not a full `SELECT`), it always runs **row-level**:

```sql
{{amount}} > 0 AND {{amount}} < 1000000

```

You can still add a join in **Advanced → Joins** for a cross-table predicate; results remain per row. See [Cross-table rules](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule/cross-table-rules.md).

#### SQL — full query[​](#sql-full-query "Direct link to SQL — full query")

When you write a full query (`SELECT … FROM {{input_view}} …`), the Condition header shows **Applies to**. Pick the level that matches what the query means.

##### Row-level[​](#row-level "Direct link to Row-level")

* Each row carries a boolean `condition` column (`TRUE` = fail).
* You must choose **Merge results back on** key columns so failures can be matched to rows of the monitored table.
* Those merge columns must appear in the query's `SELECT` list alongside `condition`.
* **Merge results back on** lives under **Advanced** and takes column slots like `{{order_id}}`, which Studio maps to the table's real columns.

```sql
SELECT
  o.{{order_id}},
  o.{{customer_id}},
  (c.id IS NULL) AS condition
FROM {{input_view}} o
LEFT JOIN catalog.schema.customers c ON o.{{customer_id}} = c.id

```

##### Dataset-level[​](#dataset-level "Direct link to Dataset-level")

* One verdict for the whole dataset (or the filtered set of rows).
* The query must aggregate to **exactly one row** and return a boolean `condition` (`TRUE` = fail). A query that returns one row per input row fails at runtime when set to dataset-level.

```sql
SELECT
  (AVG({{amount}}) < 0 OR AVG({{amount}}) > 1000000) AS condition
FROM {{input_view}}

```

Match the switch to the query

**Row-level** without merge keys, or **Dataset-level** without a single aggregated row, will fail when the rule runs. The editor warns you about these cases.

#### How this shows up in quality scores[​](#how-this-shows-up-in-quality-scores "Direct link to How this shows up in quality scores")

In the quality score, a row-level check contributes the **fraction of rows that passed** (for example 99.9% when 10 of 10,000 rows fail). A dataset-level check contributes **one pass/fail verdict**, counted a single time — never once per row, even when it flags every row in the failing group. That keeps table size from distorting the score: one dataset-wide expectation (such as "the table isn't empty") always weighs the same, instead of a huge table letting it dominate the result or a tiny one making it negligible. For how that rolls up into the DQ score, see [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md#read-the-score).


---

### Import rules

If you have data-quality rules defined somewhere else, you don't have to re-create them by hand. You can import them.

There are two ways to import: from a **DQX YAML** file, or from a **data contract**. Both do the same thing at the end — they turn what you provide into rules in your Rules Registry.

Everything lands as drafts

Nothing goes live when you import. Every imported rule arrives as a **draft**, just like a rule you write yourself. Someone must review and approve it before it can be run. See [Approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md).

#### From DQX YAML[​](#from-dqx-yaml "Direct link to From DQX YAML")

If you have rules written in DQX's own file format, paste or upload them here. This is the same format DQX Core uses to store checks, so anything exported from a DQX pipeline or checked into your code will import cleanly.

![Import rules screen, From DQX YAML tab: a box to paste or upload a YAML file, a Validate button, and a preview of the checks it found](/dqx/img/studio/import_yaml_light.png)![Import rules screen, From DQX YAML tab: a box to paste or upload a YAML file, a Validate button, and a preview of the checks it found](/dqx/img/studio/import_yaml_dark.png)

To import:

1. Paste your YAML (or JSON) into the box, or upload the file.
2. DQX Studio checks that the format is valid and shows you a preview of the rules it found. If something is wrong, you'll see exactly what needs fixing.
3. Test the rules against sample rows if you want to see how they behave before committing. No data is changed by a test.
4. Save. The rules are added to your Rules Registry as drafts.

##### Don't have YAML yet? Generate it[​](#dont-have-yaml-yet-generate-it "Direct link to Don't have YAML yet? Generate it")

If you know what you want to check but not how to write it, use the **Generate** button above the rules editor: describe the checks in plain language and DQX Studio generates the rules for you. They appear in the editor as YAML — like any pasted file — so you can read and edit them before importing; nothing is saved until you do. Rules created this way are marked as AI-assisted in the registry, and edits you make by hand clear that mark.

The option appears only when AI is configured and enabled for your workspace.

What the format looks like

The YAML format matches DQX Core's storage format for checks, so files move between the two without translation. For the full syntax — every field and option — see [Quality checks definition](/dqx/docs/guide/quality_checks_definition.md).

#### From a data contract[​](#from-a-data-contract "Direct link to From a data contract")

A **data contract** is a file that declares quality expectations for a dataset — the shape its data should take and the rules it promises to keep. DQX Studio can read [Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)](https://bitol-io.github.io/open-data-contract-standard/latest/) version 3 contracts. Instead of writing rules for a table one at a time, you can point at the contract that already describes it and let the app derive the rules for you.

The contract is owned by the team that produces the data, so it's the authoritative definition of how that data should look. Importing it turns those promises — a column that must never be empty, or must match a set of allowed values — straight into checks you can monitor, with no guessing at intent and no drift between what was agreed and what you actually test.

![Import rules screen, From a data contract tab: upload or paste an ODCS contract, then pick the Unity Catalog table each part targets](/dqx/img/studio/import_contract_light.png)![Import rules screen, From a data contract tab: upload or paste an ODCS contract, then pick the Unity Catalog table each part targets](/dqx/img/studio/import_contract_dark.png)

To import:

1. Upload or paste the ODCS v3 contract.
2. DQX Studio derives checks from it — schema validation (does each column exist with the right type?), constraints the contract sets on columns, and any explicit rules written in the contract's quality section.
3. For each part of the contract, pick the Unity Catalog table it targets, so the app knows where each rule belongs.
4. Save. The derived rules are added as drafts, ready for review.

##### Choosing what to derive[​](#choosing-what-to-derive "Direct link to Choosing what to derive")

Before you import, a few options let you control which kinds of rules DQX Studio generates from the contract. All of them are on by default.

* **Predefined rules from schema** *(on by default)* — reads the constraints the contract puts on each column and turns them into ordinary checks: *is not null* from a `required` field, *is unique* from a `unique` field, a pattern check from a `pattern`, and range or length checks from minimum/maximum/length limits. Turn it off if you only want schema validation or the contract's own explicit rules.
* **Schema validation** *(on by default)* — emits one *has valid schema* check per schema in the contract, using each column's declared type. This is the check that verifies the table actually has the columns the contract promises, with the right types.
* **Strict schema check** *(on by default)* — a sub-option of schema validation (available only when it's on). When strict, the schema check requires the **exact** column set, order, and types — nothing extra. Turn it off for permissive validation that allows additional columns and doesn't enforce order.

Import is deterministic: rules come only from the parts of a contract that are machine-checkable — property constraints and `library` or `sql` quality rules. Contracts sometimes also carry expectations written as free text (`type: text`). Those can't become a check without interpreting the prose, so they are skipped and reported in the generation warnings. To get such an expectation imported, express it in the contract as a `sql` or `library` quality rule instead, or author the check directly in Studio.

Go deeper on data contracts

For the full picture of how DQX turns a contract into checks — including the kinds of quality rules it can read — see [Data contract quality rules generation](/dqx/docs/guide/data_contract_quality_rules_generation.md).

#### Bulk import for platform teams[​](#bulk-import-for-platform-teams "Direct link to Bulk import for platform teams")

If you manage many data products and want to roll out quality rules across all of them at once — the kind of thing a platform team does from a pipeline or a Git-based workflow — DQX Studio supports **bulk import** from multiple contracts in one pass. It can register the tables, create the rules, and apply them together, so a large rollout doesn't mean importing one contract at a time.

Still reviewed

Bulk import follows the same rule: imported rules are drafts. Your team's [approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md) still applies before anything runs against production data.


---

### Rule Marketplace

The **Rule Marketplace** is a catalogue of ready-made, reusable data-quality rules — so you don't have to write the common ones from scratch. Browse rules grouped by domain, tick the ones you want, and import them into your Rules Registry as reusable templates you can map onto your tables.

Admin only

The Rule Marketplace is available to workspace **admins**. Find it in the sidebar, just above **Documentation**.

![Rule Marketplace page: industry and region filters, a search box, and domain-grouped rule packs](/dqx/img/studio/marketplace_light.png)![Rule Marketplace page: industry and region filters, a search box, and domain-grouped rule packs](/dqx/img/studio/marketplace_dark.png)

#### Browse, preview, and import[​](#browse-preview-and-import "Direct link to Browse, preview, and import")

Rules are grouped into **domain packs** — Contacts & People, Addresses & Geo, Pricing & Money, and more. Two filters narrow what's shown: **Industry** (e.g. Banking, Retail, Healthcare) and **Region** (hierarchical — choosing **EU** shows every EU rule, choosing **France** narrows to that country). The **search** box finds a rule by name across every pack.

Click a rule to expand it and see exactly what it does — its logic, parameters, and whether the row passes or fails when the condition is true. Not sure a rule behaves as you expect? Hit **Try it out** to open a test panel, type a few sample values (or point at one of your tables), and see per-row pass/fail before you import anything.

Tick the rules you want — individually, or a whole pack via its header checkbox — then click **Import *N* selected**. They land in your Rules Registry, ready to [assign to your tables](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md).

Imported rules arrive approved

Because Rule Marketplace packs are curated and the Rule Marketplace is admin-only, imported rules are **published on import** — they don't sit in the approval queue. Re-importing is safe: a rule you already have is reused, not duplicated.

#### Deploy demo content[​](#deploy-demo-content "Direct link to Deploy demo content")

Use **Deploy demo content** — the first row on the page — to deploy example tables, rules, and past run results, so you can explore the Studio with realistic data. Click the row and confirm (the default wipes existing Studio data for a clean slate); it loads in the background and takes a while, so leave it to run.

![Deploy demo content row at the top of the Rule Marketplace, with a Deploy button](/dqx/img/studio/marketplace_demo_light.png)![Deploy demo content row at the top of the Rule Marketplace, with a Deploy button](/dqx/img/studio/marketplace_demo_dark.png)

#### Contribute a pack[​](#contribute-a-pack "Direct link to Contribute a pack")

The rule packs are DQX-YAML files in the [DQX repository](https://github.com/databrickslabs/dqx/tree/main/app/src/databricks_labs_dqx_app/backend/marketplace/packs). To add a rule or a whole new domain pack, open a pull request — see the README in that directory for the format. There's a **Contribute on GitHub** link in the Rule Marketplace header too.

### Governance & security

This section is for governance admins accountable for *how* DQX Studio is run. It covers configuring the app once it's installed.

If you're setting DQX Studio up for the first time, the rollout playbook below walks you through it. For the day-to-day detail behind each step, follow the links into the rest of this section.

#### Configure DQX Studio[​](#configure-dqx-studio "Direct link to Configure DQX Studio")

You set a handful of org-wide policies once — how roles map to your teams, your approval rules, your shared standards (governed tags, quality dimensions, default thresholds), and data retention. From then on, every author, approver, and steward works within them.

You'll need the Admin role

Everything below lives under **Admin Settings** and is only available to people with the **Admin** role. If you can't see Admin Settings, ask an existing admin.

##### Step 1 — Map roles to your teams[​](#step-1--map-roles-to-your-teams "Direct link to Step 1 — Map roles to your teams")

Map your existing Databricks **workspace groups** to DQX Studio's four roles — Viewer, Rule Author, Rule Approver, Admin. Running checks is part of the Author role, so authors can run what they write; approvers review rather than run. Assign groups rather than individuals, so access follows people as they join and leave. Start narrow: most people as Viewer or Author, a small group as Approver and Admin.

![Admin Settings — Entitlements tab: workspace groups mapped to app roles](/dqx/img/studio/settings_entitlements_light.png)![Admin Settings — Entitlements tab: workspace groups mapped to app roles](/dqx/img/studio/settings_entitlements_dark.png)

Full detail: [Permissions & entitlements](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/permissions-and-entitlements.md).

##### Step 2 — Decide your approval policy[​](#step-2--decide-your-approval-policy "Direct link to Step 2 — Decide your approval policy")

By default DQX Studio uses **four-eyes approval**: an author submits a draft and someone else approves it before it goes live. Keep this on for production; for a sandbox you can allow auto-approval. The setting is itself audited.

![Admin Settings — Governance tab: approvals mode and data retention](/dqx/img/studio/settings_governance_thumb_light.png)![Admin Settings — Governance tab: approvals mode and data retention](/dqx/img/studio/settings_governance_thumb_dark.png)

Full detail: [The approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md).

##### Step 3 — Define your standards[​](#step-3--define-your-standards "Direct link to Step 3 — Define your standards")

Set the shared vocabulary authors will reuse:

* **Governed tags** — reusable labels such as `domain`, `pii`, or `class.location`. These are defined in **Unity Catalog**, not in DQX Studio, and authors pick from them (or create their own in Unity Catalog) when tagging a rule's column. A tagged rule then auto-applies to matching columns. See [Governed tags](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md#governed-tags).
* **Quality dimensions** — the categories you report against (completeness, validity, accuracy, consistency, uniqueness, timeliness).
* **Default pass thresholds** — how strict a check must be to count as passing. Set a sensible default; authors can override per table. See [Set quality thresholds](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md#quality-thresholds).

##### Step 4 — Set retention and handle sensitive data[​](#step-4--set-retention-and-handle-sensitive-data "Direct link to Step 4 — Set retention and handle sensitive data")

In Admin Settings you choose how long runs, results, and metrics are kept, and — separately — how long quarantined rows (which may contain sensitive data) are kept. Keep the evidence long enough to investigate, then let it clear to minimize the app data.

Now invite your team

With roles, approvals, and standards in place, point authors at the [Quickstart](/dqx/docs/studio/quickstart.md) and stewards at [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md).

#### How DQX Studio respects your data access[​](#how-dqx-studio-respects-your-data-access "Direct link to How DQX Studio respects your data access")

DQX Studio browses Unity Catalog **on your behalf** — you only ever see catalogs and tables you already have permission to, and profiling and tests run under your own access. It never widens anyone's permissions. Quarantined rows are visible only to approvers and admins, and still only for data they can already read.

Every change to a rule, role, permission, or schedule is **audited** — who changed it, when, and the before-and-after values. Review a rule's history on its **History** tab (and a collection's on the collection's **History** tab); the complete trail is kept in append-only history tables in the app's own catalog.

#### In this section[​](#in-this-section "Direct link to In this section")

* [Permissions & entitlements](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/permissions-and-entitlements.md) — roles across the app, and per-object access.
* [The approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md) — draft → review → approve, and the four-eyes rule.
* [Try the built-in demo](/dqx/docs/demos.md#dqx-studio) — deploy sample content from Admin Settings to explore every feature.
