### The approval workflow (four-eyes)

Every rule, monitored table, and collection moves through the same simple states before it can affect a run:

1. **Draft** — someone is authoring or editing it. No effect on any run yet.
2. **Submitted for review** — the author is done and asks for a second pair of eyes.
3. **Approved / active** — a reviewer has approved it. It's now live and runnable.

A reviewer can also send a submission back to draft with a reason, so the author can fix it and resubmit.

<!-- -->

#### The four-eyes principle[​](#the-four-eyes-principle "Direct link to The four-eyes principle")

**An author can't approve their own submission** unless they're also an approver or admin. In practice at least two people touch every change — the person who wrote it and the person who approved it. A second reviewer catches the obvious slips (a typo in a column name, a threshold set too high, a check on the wrong table) before they reach a live run.

Small teams aren't blocked

Approvers and admins can approve their own drafts, so a small team isn't stuck. The rule only stops authors *without* approval rights from self-approving.

#### The reviewer experience[​](#the-reviewer-experience "Direct link to The reviewer experience")

**Review & Approve** is your approval queue: every pending rule, table, and collection awaiting your decision, gathered in one place. For any item, choose **View changes** to see the proposed definition. If it already has a live version you'll see a **diff** against what's active today.

![Review & Approve page listing a pending rule with Approve, Reject, and View changes actions](/dqx/img/studio/review_approve_light.png)![Review & Approve page listing a pending rule with Approve, Reject, and View changes actions](/dqx/img/studio/review_approve_dark.png)

From there you can **test it** against sample rows first (nothing is changed or saved), **approve** it with a comment (it becomes active and counts in the next run), or **reject** it with a reason (it returns to the author as a draft). Every approval and rejection is recorded — who acted, when, and what changed.

#### The author experience[​](#the-author-experience "Direct link to The author experience")

When your draft is ready, choose **Submit for review**, then track its status: pending, approved and active, or sent back. If it's rejected, it returns as a draft with the reviewer's reason attached — fix what they flagged and resubmit.

Editing an active item is safe

Editing something that's already active creates a new draft version. The live version keeps working until your edit is reviewed and approved, so you can't accidentally disrupt a running check while you tweak it.

#### When approvals are turned off[​](#when-approvals-are-turned-off "Direct link to When approvals are turned off")

An admin decides whether approvals are **required** (recommended for anything feeding real reporting) or **off** (auto-approve, suited to a trusted or development environment). When they're off, the review queue is hidden and submissions go live immediately. This choice is itself an audited admin setting — set it when you [configure DQX Studio](/dqx/docs/studio/governance.md).


---

### Permissions & Entitlements

Two different securables control what you can do in DQX Studio, and it helps to keep them apart:

* **Entitlements** are your **roles across the whole app** — whether you can view rules, write them, approve them, or change settings.
* **Permissions** are your **access permissions to one specific object** — a single rule, monitored table, or collection.

Your entitlement follows you everywhere; permissions apply object by object.

#### Workspace and data access[​](#workspace-and-data-access "Direct link to Workspace and data access")

[Beta](/dqx/docs/reference/feature_lifecycle.md#beta "Feature lifecycle: Beta")[Available since DQX v0.17.0](https://github.com/databrickslabs/dqx/releases/tag/v0.17.0 "Available since DQX v0.17.0")

In-app roles and object permissions do **not** grant Databricks App access, warehouse access, or Unity Catalog privileges. Those come from the installation, which an administrator sets up once and which Studio verifies.

Breaking change: fresh installs only

There is no upgrade path from earlier Studio installations. Remove the previous app, task-runner job, warehouse, Unity Catalog schemas, and Lakebase project, then install this release fresh. Broad access granted by earlier versions (`users` / `account users`) is not revoked automatically; review and remove it.

##### Minimal setup[​](#minimal-setup "Direct link to Minimal setup")

**From the Marketplace.**

1. Install the listing and bind a SQL warehouse and a Lakebase endpoint.
2. Share the app with the audience group and the administrator group (**Compute → Apps → DQX Studio → Permissions → Can Use**). This is a manual step.
3. Open Studio as a workspace administrator (a member of `admins` or of the configured admin group).
4. In the setup form, enter the **catalog**, a **storage prefix** (default `dqx_studio`), and the **audience group** (an existing dedicated group).
5. Run the `GRANT` statements that setup prints, then choose **Verify again**.
6. In **Admin Settings → Entitlements**, assign roles to the audience groups.

After the first successful full verification, app restarts reuse it only for catalog-level grants (`USE CATALOG` / `CREATE SCHEMA` on the selected catalog) that the app service principal cannot inspect itself; a changed audience, catalog, or task runner, or any grant observed missing, requires an administrator to choose **Verify again**.

**From a bundle (DAB).** Deploy with `make app-deploy PROFILE=<profile> TARGET=<target> STUDIO_PREFIX=<prefix> STUDIO_USER_GROUP=<group|users>`, grant the catalog prerequisites that setup prints, and assign roles. The bundle supplies catalog, prefix, and audience, so setup shows them read-only and skips the form. See the [installation guide](/dqx/docs/installation.md#dqx-studio-installation).

##### Storage layout[​](#storage-layout "Direct link to Storage layout")

Studio uses an existing catalog and a prefix (lower-case letters, digits, and underscores; default `dqx_studio`):

| Object            | Purpose                                    |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `<prefix>`        | Main Studio schema                         |
| `<prefix>.wheels` | Volume for the app and task-runner wheels  |
| `<prefix>_tmp`    | Temporary views created on behalf of users |
| `<prefix>_genie`  | Approved Genie views and metadata          |
| `<prefix>_demo`   | Demo content                               |

Catalog and prefix cannot be changed once storage exists. The Lakebase schema does not follow the prefix.

##### Who gets what[​](#who-gets-what "Direct link to Who gets what")

Setup applies the access below, then **re-reads it to verify**. A missing grant, or one that cannot be inspected, blocks readiness. The only exception is sharing the app itself: if Studio cannot read the app's sharing it shows a warning rather than blocking (administrators see it in a dismissible banner once Studio is ready), and you share the app manually. ACL changes are additive, so unrelated principals on shared resources are preserved.

| Resource                    | App SP                                                  | Runner SP                                   | Audience                                 | Admin group             |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Catalog                     | `USE CATALOG`, `CREATE SCHEMA`                          | `USE CATALOG`                               | `USE CATALOG`                            | `USE CATALOG`           |
| Main schema                 | Owner (Marketplace); explicit list incl. `MANAGE` (DAB) | `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT`, `MODIFY`            | None                                     | None                    |
| Wheels volume               | Owner / `ALL_PRIVILEGES`                                | `READ VOLUME`                               | None                                     | None                    |
| `_tmp` schema               | Owner / explicit list incl. `MANAGE`                    | `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT` (any view in `_tmp`) | `USE SCHEMA`, `CREATE TABLE`             | Same as audience        |
| `_genie` schema             | Owner / explicit list incl. `MANAGE`                    | None                                        | `USE SCHEMA`; `SELECT` on allowlist only | Same as audience        |
| `_demo` schema              | Owner (Marketplace); explicit list incl. `MANAGE` (DAB) | None                                        | `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT`                   | Same as audience        |
| SQL warehouse               | `CAN_MANAGE`                                            | Not needed                                  | `CAN_USE`                                | `CAN_USE`               |
| App                         | Runtime identity                                        | None                                        | `CAN_USE`                                | `CAN_USE`               |
| Task-runner job             | `CAN_MANAGE`                                            | Configured `run_as`                         | None                                     | Managed via setup       |
| Genie space (if configured) | Manage                                                  | None                                        | `CAN_RUN`                                | `CAN_RUN`               |
| Dashboard (if configured)   | Publisher; `CAN_MANAGE` on the bundle dashboard (DAB)   | None                                        | `CAN_READ`                               | `CAN_READ`              |
| Lakebase app schema         | Owner, migrations, CRUD                                 | None                                        | None                                     | None                    |
| User source data            | Authorized scheduled workloads only                     | Run-specific verified access                | Caller's own OBO access                  | Caller's own OBO access |

The Genie `SELECT` allowlist is exactly the five approved views plus `dim_dq_rules` and `dim_dq_monitored_tables`. Studio never grants whole-schema Genie `SELECT`, quarantine tables, or `dq_user_table_entitlements`. On a bundle deployment the schemas are owned by the deploying identity, so the app service principal receives an explicit privilege list that includes `MANAGE` (not `ALL_PRIVILEGES`, which makes the bundle engine drop `MANAGE`) instead. The bundle grants the administrator group only its workspace permissions; the app re-applies and verifies the administrator group's Unity Catalog grants after each deploy restart.

The runner service principal needs no Lakebase role or grants. Run configs too large to pass as job parameters are staged in the Delta `dq_run_configs` table in the main schema, which its main-schema `SELECT` / `MODIFY` already covers.

##### Audience, broad mode, and administrators[​](#audience-broad-mode-and-administrators "Direct link to Audience, broad mode, and administrators")

The **audience** is a dedicated, existing workspace group. Studio never creates groups, and the setup form rejects `users`, `account users`, and `admins`.

**Broad mode** (bundle deployments only, `STUDIO_USER_GROUP=users`) shares the app, warehouse, dashboard, and Genie space with the workspace `users` group and grants Unity Catalog access to `account users`. That is **account-wide**: everyone in the account can reach the Studio catalog objects. Use it only when that is intended.

| Audience input                   | Workspace ACL principal | Unity Catalog principal |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `users` (bundle broad mode only) | `users`                 | `account users`         |
| Dedicated group                  | Group name              | Same group name         |

**Administrator access.** Members of the configured admin group **or** the workspace `admins` group may run setup. Unity Catalog cannot grant to the workspace `admins` group, so Unity Catalog grants for administrators go only to a **custom** admin account group, which receives the same access as the audience plus app `CAN_USE`. With the built-in `admins` group, administrators must also be members of the audience group to use features that run on their behalf. Audience membership never makes someone an in-app Admin.

##### What stays per user[​](#what-stays-per-user "Direct link to What stays per user")

Some access cannot be proven for a whole group, so it is checked for the active user when they use the feature: their **Databricks SQL access entitlement**, their **OAuth consent** for Studio's scopes (sign in again if a scope changes), and their own **source-data privileges** on the tables they profile or validate. Studio never grants source data.

Profiling and validation use your data permissions to create a temporary view, then grant `MANAGE` on that view to the app service principal for cleanup. The job runner reads the view through schema-level `SELECT` on the temporary schema, so it can read any view in that schema. Schedules verify source catalog/schema usage and `SELECT` for the app scheduler and runner; failed runner grants block scheduling. The schedule editor lists any missing catalog or schema usage by service principal name, with the `GRANT` statements an owner needs to run. Setting up a schedule needs `MANAGE` (or ownership) on each table it reads, except tables in the built-in `samples` catalog, which need no grants. Ask Genie additionally requires space `CAN_RUN`, Consumer access or Databricks SQL access entitlement, and the approved-view grants above.

#### Entitlements (your role)[​](#entitlements-your-role "Direct link to Entitlements (your role)")

Every person has one of four roles. **Author and Approver are complementary, not ranked** — an author writes and runs rules, an approver signs off on them, and the two are deliberately kept apart so that [four-eyes review](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md) works. Only an **Admin** can do everything.

| Task                                                  | Viewer | Rule Author | Rule Approver | Admin |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ----------- | ------------- | ----- |
| View rules, tables, collections, and results          | ✅     | ✅          | ✅            | ✅    |
| Create rules and edit your own drafts                 |        | ✅          |               | ✅    |
| Submit drafts for approval                            |        | ✅          |               | ✅    |
| Run checks (profiling & validation)                   |        | ✅          |               | ✅    |
| Approve or reject anyone's drafts                     |        |             | ✅            | ✅    |
| Change admin settings (entitlements, retention, tags) |        |             |               | ✅    |

You don't get a role by name. An admin maps your **Databricks workspace groups** to DQX Studio roles in **Admin Settings → Entitlements**; if your groups map you to more than one role, the **highest wins**. Your **Profile** page (top-right menu) lists the Databricks workspace groups you belong to — the groups this mapping draws on.

![Admin Settings Entitlements tab, mapping workspace groups to DQX Studio roles](/dqx/img/studio/settings_entitlements_light.png)![Admin Settings Entitlements tab, mapping workspace groups to DQX Studio roles](/dqx/img/studio/settings_entitlements_dark.png)

#### Permissions (per-object access)[​](#permissions-per-object-access "Direct link to Permissions (per-object access)")

Every rule, monitored table, and collection has its own **Permissions tab** showing who the **Steward** is (the accountable owner for that object's data quality) and a list of who has access. You grant each **principal** — a user or a workspace group — one or more privileges on **that object only**:

* **View** (SELECT) — see the object and its results.
* **Modify** — edit the object's configuration and logic, and delete it.
* **Apply** — attach the object to others (apply a rule to a table, add a table to a collection).
* **Execute** — run profiling and validation on this **table or collection** (Execute doesn't apply to rules).
* **ALL PRIVILEGES** — the full set, including managing the object's permissions.

Anything you can act on you can also see, so Modify, Apply, or Execute include View privilege automatically.

Running needs both a role and Execute

Triggering a run takes the **Rule Author** or **Admin** role *and* the **Execute** permission on the specific table or collection. Admins and approvers reach every object regardless of its permission list, so governance can never be locked out.

##### Defaults and cascade[​](#defaults-and-cascade "Direct link to Defaults and cascade")

When you create an object — a rule, monitored table, or collection — nothing is blocked out of the box: **you become the owner** with ALL PRIVILEGES, and **all workspace users** get View, Apply, and Execute (Modify is held back). These defaults are real entries on the object's **Permissions tab**, not hard-coded behavior — so you can narrow them to specific groups, or remove them, whenever you like.

By default permissions **cascade** through the hierarchy — granting access on a collection also grants it on the collection's tables and their applied rules. Admins control whether cascade is on by default in **Admin Settings → Entitlements**.

Changes are audited

Role changes and object-permission changes are all recorded — who made the change, when, and the before-and-after values.


---

### Load checks outside the app

You author and approve rules in DQX Studio, but you don't have to run them there. Studio keeps its rules in own catalog, so they can be loaded and run outside the app — no export needed.

Studio exposes its **approved** rules through a dqx-core-compatible view, `dq_rules_core`, that the standard [DQX Core](/dqx/docs/guide.md) `DQEngine.load_checks` API reads directly.

#### Load approved rules[​](#load-approved-rules "Direct link to Load approved rules")

Point `LakebaseChecksStorageConfig` at the view and pass the table you want the rules for as `run_config_name`:

```python
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from databricks.labs.dqx.engine import DQEngine
from databricks.labs.dqx.config import LakebaseChecksStorageConfig

engine = DQEngine(WorkspaceClient())

checks: list[dict] = engine.load_checks(
    LakebaseChecksStorageConfig(
        # <lakebase-database>.<studio-schema>.dq_rules_core
        location="databricks_postgres.dqx_studio.dq_rules_core",
        instance_name="<your-lakebase-instance>",   # Studio's Lakebase instance
        run_config_name="main.sales.orders",        # the table the rules apply to
    )
)

# Run the Studio-authored rules against your own DataFrame
checked_df = engine.apply_checks_by_metadata(df, checks)

```

Only **approved** rules are loaded — drafts and rejected rules are never returned. You get the table's current approved set, so no version pinning is needed. There's no argument for loading a single rule; if you want just one, filter the returned list in your own code.

Cross-table SQL checks have no single home table and appear under `__sql_check__/<name>` instead of a table name.

Access you'll need

`dq_rules_core` lives in Studio's **Lakebase Postgres** database, so a reader outside the app — an engineer, or a pipeline's service principal — needs an administrator to grant two things:

* **`CAN_USE`** on the Lakebase database instance, so the reader can connect to it (see the Databricks [database instance permissions](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/oltp/) docs).

* A Postgres `SELECT` on the view:

  ```sql
  GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA dqx_studio TO "<principal>";
  GRANT SELECT ON dqx_studio.dq_rules_core TO "<principal>";

  ```

`dqx_studio` here is Studio's Lakebase schema (`lakebase_schema_name`, default `dqx_studio`). It does not follow the Unity Catalog storage prefix. `<principal>` is the Postgres role for the reader's identity — for a service principal, its **application id**. `SELECT` on the view is enough; readers don't need access to the underlying `dq_resolved_rules` table.

When a **service principal** does the reading (for example a scheduled pipeline), also set `client_id` to its application id on the `LakebaseChecksStorageConfig` so the connection authenticates as that SP — `client_id="<service-principal-application-id>"`. A user running `load_checks` interactively omits `client_id`, and the connection uses their own identity.

#### Notes and limits[​](#notes-and-limits "Direct link to Notes and limits")

* **Approved only.** The view excludes drafts and rejected rules by design — approve a rule in Studio before a pipeline can load it.
* **Read-only.** `dq_rules_core` is a view: author and manage rules in the app; pipelines only read.
* **No version pinning.** The `dq_rules_core` view exposes only the currently approved rules and recomputes `rule_set_fingerprint` from them, so a table has just one fingerprint at any moment — there's no history to load. Passing an older `rule_set_fingerprint` to `load_checks` returns an empty list, so it's only useful to confirm the set hasn't changed since you last loaded it, not to retrieve a past version. (Version pinning does work when dqx-core owns the rules table directly, rather than through Studio's view.)


---

### Monitor your tables

This section is for stewards who want to put real, ongoing data-quality checks on a table. It's where the reusable rules in your [Rules Registry](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md) stop being definitions and start doing work.

When you apply rules to a Unity Catalog table, that table becomes a **monitored table** — the single source of truth for that table's data quality. Everything about how healthy the table is, which checks run on it, and how it's trended over time lives in one place.

#### Open a table to monitor[​](#open-a-table-to-monitor "Direct link to Open a table to monitor")

1. Go to **Tables**.
2. Select **Monitor a table**.
3. Browse Unity Catalog: pick a **catalog** > **schema** > **table**. You only see catalogs, schemas, and tables you already have access to — if a table you expect isn't listed, you are missing a permission.
4. The table detail opens.

Adding many tables at once

Need to bring dozens of tables under monitoring? Use bulk-register to add many tables in one step instead of opening them one at a time.

#### The table detail[​](#the-table-detail "Direct link to The table detail")

A monitored table has four tabs:

* **About** — the table's schema, a preview of sample data, and an "ask a question" box for quick natural-language questions about the data.
* **Apply Rules** — where you turn rules into live checks. See [Assign rules](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md).
* **Results** — the table's data-quality score, its trend over time, and a breakdown you can drill down to the failing rows. See [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md).
* **Profile** — a scan of the table's shape that can suggest candidate rules. See [Profiling](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/profiling.md).

![Monitored table About tab showing schema, a governed tag, and a sample-data preview with an ask-a-question box](/dqx/img/studio/table_detail_light.png)![Monitored table About tab showing schema, a governed tag, and a sample-data preview with an ask-a-question box](/dqx/img/studio/table_detail_dark.png)

#### In this section[​](#in-this-section "Direct link to In this section")

* **[Assign rules](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md)** — attach rules from your registry to a table's columns, tune them per table, and set [quality thresholds](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md#quality-thresholds).
* **[Profiling](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/profiling.md)** — scan a table and let the DQX suggest candidate rules.
* **[Collections](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/collections.md)** — group related tables into a data product or domain and see quality across all of them at once.
* **[Run checks & schedule](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/run-and-schedule.md)** — run checks on demand or on a schedule, and see past runs.


---

### Assign rules

Assigning rules is where the reusable definitions in your [Rules Registry](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md) start doing work: you attach them to a [monitored table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring.md)'s columns and tune them for that table. Each rule you apply to a column becomes a **check** — a single rule can become many checks across your tables and columns.

Open the **Apply Rules** tab on a monitored table to get started.

![Apply Rules tab showing rules mapped to columns, severity indicators, pass-threshold badges, and a Suggest rules button](/dqx/img/studio/table_apply_rules_light.png)![Apply Rules tab showing rules mapped to columns, severity indicators, pass-threshold badges, and a Suggest rules button](/dqx/img/studio/table_apply_rules_dark.png)

You can look at your checks two ways:

* **By column** — see every check attached to a given column.
* **By rule** — see every column a given rule is checking.

For each check you apply, you can tune it for this table without touching the underlying rule:

* **Override the severity.** Set how much a failure matters on this table — **Low**, **Medium**, **High**, or **Critical**. The rule carries a default severity; you can override it here. Severity is a priority for triage and reporting, not what decides pass or fail. See [Severity](/dqx/docs/studio.md#severity).
* **Set a pass threshold.** Instead of demanding every row pass, you can require, say, 70% of rows to pass for the check to count as healthy. See [Quality thresholds](#quality-thresholds) below.

#### Pin a rule version[​](#pin-a-rule-version "Direct link to Pin a rule version")

Rules in the registry evolve — an author edits a rule and it gets a new version. Each check on your table shows a **version selector** (for example, *Latest (v1)*). You choose how that check tracks the rule:

* **Latest** — the check always uses the newest approved version of the rule, so improvements roll out to your table automatically.
* **Pin to a version** — lock the check to a specific version, so it stays exactly as it is until you deliberately move it. Pin when you want a table's behavior to stay stable regardless of registry changes.

Pinning is per check, so you can let most checks follow the latest while holding a sensitive one steady.

#### Quality thresholds[​](#quality-thresholds "Direct link to Quality thresholds")

Real data is rarely perfect. By default a check either passes or fails, so a column that's 88% clean fails a check that demands 100% — and may stay red forever. A check that's always red is one people learn to ignore. A **pass threshold** sets how many rows must pass for the check to count as green. Set it to `< 90%` and the check needs 90% of rows to pass; a small badge on the check shows the bar.

This turns quality into a dial instead of a pass/fail cliff. Set the threshold just below where the data is today so the check goes green, then raise it — to 95%, then 98% — each time the data improves. A steadily rising threshold is a much clearer signal of progress than a check stuck on red. Thresholds are set per rule and per column, right here on the Apply Rules tab, and admins can set a sensible org-wide default that authors override per check (see [Set up for your org](/dqx/docs/studio/governance.md)).

Thresholds change flagging, not the score or your data

A pass threshold only decides when a check is *flagged* as failing in the UI. It never edits or deletes rows, and it doesn't change the numeric DQ score — a check at 82% still contributes 0.82 whether or not it clears its threshold. See [how the score works](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md#read-the-score).

#### Suggest rules with AI[​](#suggest-rules-with-ai "Direct link to Suggest rules with AI")

You don't have to map every check by hand. Select **Suggest rules** and DQX Studio looks at this specific table — its columns, their names and types, and the shape of the data — and proposes a tailored set of checks for it: an `id` that should be unique, an `email` that should match a pattern, an `amount` that shouldn't be negative, and so on.

![Suggest rules with AI: the app proposes a tailored set of checks for a table's columns](/dqx/img/studio/feat_suggest_light.png)![Suggest rules with AI: the app proposes a tailored set of checks for a table's columns](/dqx/img/studio/feat_suggest_dark.png)

It's the fastest way to go from an unmonitored table to a sensible starting set of checks. You stay in control — review each suggestion, keep the ones that fit, drop the rest, and adjust severities or thresholds before you submit. Think of it as a knowledgeable first draft of "what should we be checking on this table?", not a decision made for you.

Governed tags apply rules automatically

If a rule's column is marked with a governed tag (for example `class.location`), that rule is applied automatically to any column on this table carrying the same tag — so tagged rules land on the right columns without you mapping them by hand. See [Governed tags](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md#governed-tags).

Your data is never changed

Applying rules and running checks only reads and evaluates your data. A failing check never deletes or modifies the table — the failing rows are copied to a quarantine table for triage.

#### Save as draft, or submit for review[​](#save-as-draft-or-submit-for-review "Direct link to Save as draft, or submit for review")

When you've applied the checks you want, you can click **save as a draft** to keep working, or **submit for review**. Once your changes are approved, the table is actively monitored and its checks run on the schedule set for it.

* Learn how review and approval works in the [Approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md).
* Learn how and when checks run in [Run checks & schedule](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/run-and-schedule.md).


---

### Collections (data products)

This page is for stewards who own a data product or domain — a set of related tables that people rely on together. A **collection** groups those tables so you can see, run, and report on their quality as a single unit.

A collection is more than a place to schedule runs. Its real value is a single view of quality **across related tables**: the tables that feed one Genie space, one dashboard, or one published data product. Instead of checking each table on its own, you open the collection and see how the whole product is doing at once.

You don't need a collection to start

Begin by monitoring a table or two. When you have a few related tables you want to run and report on together, group them into a collection. Collections are totally optional.

#### A concrete example[​](#a-concrete-example "Direct link to A concrete example")

Say your organization publishes a **Customer 360** data product — a combined customer view backed by three tables: `customers`, `orders`, and `payments`. Each is a monitored table with its own rules. On their own, you'd check three separate scores.

Group them into a **Customer 360** collection and you get one Results view: the combined quality of the data behind that product, plus the ability to run all three together and drill into whichever table is dragging the score down.

![Collections list showing collections such as Fulfillment and Customer 360 with table counts, rule counts, check counts, and a data-quality score for each](/dqx/img/studio/collections_list_light.png)![Collections list showing collections such as Fulfillment and Customer 360 with table counts, rule counts, check counts, and a data-quality score for each](/dqx/img/studio/collections_list_dark.png)

#### Create a collection[​](#create-a-collection "Direct link to Create a collection")

1. Go to **Collections**.
2. Select **New collection**.
3. Give it a name and a short description that says what data product it represents — for example, "Customer, order and payment data for the customer view."
4. Add the related monitored tables as **members**. You add tables you already monitor, so their rules and checks come along automatically.

Collection consists of monitored tables

A collection is built from tables you're already monitoring. If a table isn't listed when you add members, monitor it first — see [Monitor a table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring.md).

#### View combined Results[​](#view-combined-results "Direct link to View combined Results")

Open the collection's **Results** tab to see quality across every member table at once:

* **A combined score** — one data-quality score for the whole product, rolled up from its member tables.
* **Trend over time** — a multi-series chart so you can see each member's quality move together (or apart) across runs.
* **Breakdowns** — score by dimension (completeness, validity, and so on), by severity (Low / Medium / High / Critical), by rule, and by member table.
* **Drill-down** — select a member table to open its own Results and follow the score down to the failing rows.

![Collection Results tab showing a combined average score across member tables, an over-time multi-series chart, score broken down by dimension and severity, and an Ask Genie box](/dqx/img/studio/collection_results_light.png)![Collection Results tab showing a combined average score across member tables, an over-time multi-series chart, score broken down by dimension and severity, and an Ask Genie box](/dqx/img/studio/collection_results_dark.png)

For how the score is calculated and how to read the breakdowns, see [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md).

Ask Genie about your quality

The Results view has an **Ask Genie** box. Ask questions about the collection's quality in plain English — for example, "which table failed the most checks last week?" — and get an answer without writing any SQL.

#### Run the collection[​](#run-the-collection "Direct link to Run the collection")

You can run every member table's checks together, on demand or on a schedule.

* **Run now** — trigger a run of the whole collection whenever you want, so all members are evaluated against the same point in time.
* **On a schedule** — set the collection to run **hourly**, **daily**, or **weekly**, or on a custom **cron** schedule for finer control. You can **pause**, **resume**, or **delete** a schedule at any time.

Running a collection requires the **Rule Author** (or Admin) role and **Execute** permission on the collection. For the full picture of how runs work, see [Run checks & schedule](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/run-and-schedule.md).

#### Publish a stable version[​](#publish-a-stable-version "Direct link to Publish a stable version")

Approving a collection **publishes a version** of it: a stable snapshot of its member tables and the rules applied to them. That version is what runs on the schedule, so your reporting stays steady even while you draft changes.

Changes to a collection go through the same review as everything else — see the [Approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md).


---

### Load and run checks in a pipeline

You author and approve rules in DQX Studio, but you don't have to run them there. Studio keeps its rules in your own workspace, so they can be loaded and run outside the app with DQX Core — no export needed.

Studio exposes its **approved** rules through a dqx-core-compatible view, `dq_rules_core`, that the standard [DQX Core](/dqx/docs/guide.md) `DQEngine.load_checks` API reads directly.

#### Load approved rules[​](#load-approved-rules "Direct link to Load approved rules")

Point `LakebaseChecksStorageConfig` at the view and pass the table you want the rules for as `run_config_name`:

```python
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from databricks.labs.dqx.engine import DQEngine
from databricks.labs.dqx.config import LakebaseChecksStorageConfig

engine = DQEngine(WorkspaceClient())

checks: list[dict] = engine.load_checks(
    LakebaseChecksStorageConfig(
        # <lakebase-database>.<studio-schema>.dq_rules_core
        location="databricks_postgres.dqx_studio.dq_rules_core",
        instance_name="<your-lakebase-instance>",   # Studio's Lakebase instance
        run_config_name="main.sales.orders",        # the table the rules apply to
    )
)

# Run the Studio-authored rules against your own DataFrame
checked_df = engine.apply_checks_by_metadata(df, checks)

```

Only **approved** rules are loaded — drafts and rejected rules are never returned. You get the table's current approved set, so no version pinning is needed. There's no argument for loading a single rule; if you want just one, filter the returned list in your own code.

Cross-table SQL checks have no single home table and appear under `__sql_check__/<name>` instead of a table name.

Access you'll need

`dq_rules_core` lives in Studio's **Lakebase Postgres** database, so a reader outside the app — an engineer, or a pipeline's service principal — needs an administrator to grant two things:

* **`CAN_USE`** on the Lakebase database instance, so the reader can connect to it (see the Databricks [database instance permissions](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/oltp/) docs).

* A Postgres `SELECT` on the view:

  ```sql
  GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA dqx_studio TO "<principal>";
  GRANT SELECT ON dqx_studio.dq_rules_core TO "<principal>";

  ```

`dqx_studio` here is Studio's Lakebase schema (`lakebase_schema_name`, default `dqx_studio`). It does not follow the Unity Catalog storage prefix. `<principal>` is the Postgres role for the reader's identity — for a service principal, its **application id**. `SELECT` on the view is enough; readers don't need access to the underlying `dq_resolved_rules` table.

When a **service principal** does the reading (for example a scheduled pipeline), also set `client_id` to its application id on the `LakebaseChecksStorageConfig` so the connection authenticates as that SP — `client_id="<service-principal-application-id>"`. A user running `load_checks` interactively omits `client_id`, and the connection uses their own identity.

#### Notes and limits[​](#notes-and-limits "Direct link to Notes and limits")

* **Approved only.** The view excludes drafts and rejected rules by design — approve a rule in Studio before a pipeline can load it.
* **Read-only.** `dq_rules_core` is a view: author and manage rules in the app; pipelines only read.
* **No version pinning.** The `dq_rules_core` view exposes only the currently approved rules and recomputes `rule_set_fingerprint` from them, so a table has just one fingerprint at any moment — there's no history to load. Passing an older `rule_set_fingerprint` to `load_checks` returns an empty list, so it's only useful to confirm the set hasn't changed since you last loaded it, not to retrieve a past version. (Version pinning does work when dqx-core owns the rules table directly, rather than through Studio's view.)

### Profiling

If you're not sure what rules a particular table needs, let DQX profile the data and suggest them. **Profiling** scans a table, measures the shape of what's actually in it, and suggests candidate rules based on what it finds. You review the suggestions and keep the ones that make sense.

It's the data-driven way to get a starting set of rules without writing them from scratch. Open the **Profile** tab on a [monitored table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring.md) to run it.

![The Profile tab: per-column completeness and distinct-value statistics, with a panel of suggested candidate rules grouped by check type](/dqx/img/studio/profiling_light.png)![The Profile tab: per-column completeness and distinct-value statistics, with a panel of suggested candidate rules grouped by check type](/dqx/img/studio/profiling_dark.png)

#### What profiling does[​](#what-profiling-does "Direct link to What profiling does")

Profiling reads a sample of the table and computes statistics for each column, such as:

* how many rows there are
* how often a column is blank or empty
* how many distinct values a column has
* the minimum and maximum values
* the most common values, and
* patterns it detects in the values (for example, values that look like email addresses)

From those statistics it proposes **candidate rules** — draft rule ideas drawn from the data, e.g.:

* a column that's never blank becomes a suggested **"is not null"** check
* values that all match an email shape become a suggested **pattern** check
* a column with a small set of repeated values becomes a suggested **"is in list"** check

These are suggestions, not decisions. You decide which ones to keep.

#### Run the profiler[​](#run-the-profiler "Direct link to Run the profiler")

1. Open the table's **Profile** tab. You can only profile tables you already have access to in Unity Catalog.
2. Run the profiler. It runs on behalf of you (OBO), reads a sample of the data, and computes the statistics above.
3. Review the results. You'll see two things: the **profiler statistics** (the measured shape of each column) and the **suggested candidate rules** drawn from them. Read the statistics to sanity-check each suggestion — a "never blank" column is only worth an "is not null" check if that will stay true.
4. Keep the suggestions you want. Retained suggestions are saved as **drafts** so you can refine them before they go live.
5. You can discard the rest.

Your data isn't touched

Profiling only reads a sample and computes statistics — it never changes, deletes, or moves your data. And a suggested rule doesn't take effect on its own: it lands as a draft and still goes through the normal review and approval steps before it starts checking data.

#### Profiling or Suggest rules with AI?[​](#profiling-or-suggest-rules-with-ai "Direct link to Profiling or Suggest rules with AI?")

Both help you write rules faster, in different ways:

* **Profiling is statistics-driven.** It measures what's actually in the table and proposes rules from those numbers. Use it when you want to see the shape of the data alongside each suggestion.
* **[Suggest rules with AI](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md#suggest-rules-with-ai)** reads the table's columns and data and proposes a tailored set of checks directly on the Apply Rules tab. Use it when you want the fastest path to a sensible starting set.


---

### Run checks & schedule

A **run** evaluates every check on a table (or a whole collection) against the current data and records the results. You can run checks on demand or on a schedule.

#### Run now[​](#run-now "Direct link to Run now")

Open a monitored table or a collection and click **Run now**. The run continues in the background, so you can leave the page. When it finishes it appears in **Runs History** with its status and duration, and its results show up on the [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md) view.

**Run now** (and every scheduled run) always evaluates the **full table** — it never samples. These are the runs your real, ongoing monitoring relies on: because they cover every row, their scores and failing-row counts are exact. To try unpublished changes cheaply, use **Run draft** below, which samples.

Who can run checks

Running is part of the **Rule Author** role (Admins can run too); Approvers and Viewers can't. You also need the **Execute** permission on this particular table or collection. See [Permissions & entitlements](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/permissions-and-entitlements.md).

#### Run draft[​](#run-draft "Direct link to Run draft")

While you still have unpublished changes, use **Run draft** to try the live applied-rule set before you submit for review.

Draft runs sample by default so large tables stay cheap to explore:

* **Default sample size:** 1000 rows
* Change the sample next to **Run draft** (random sample of N rows, or full table)
* Choosing **Full table** scans every row, same as a published run

The sample control appears on the monitored-table and collection pages whenever a draft run is available.

#### Put it on a schedule[​](#put-it-on-a-schedule "Direct link to Put it on a schedule")

For quality you want to keep an eye on, put a collection (or a single table) on a schedule so it runs itself — **hourly**, **daily** at a time you pick, **weekly** on chosen days, or a **custom** cron expression. You can **pause**, **resume**, or **delete** a schedule at any time. Scheduled times follow the workspace timezone set by your admin, and if a scheduled run is still going when the next one is due, the app skips the new one rather than running two at once.

Open the **Schedule** tab on a monitored table or collection to configure:

* **Cadence** — hourly, daily, weekly, or a custom cron
* **Timezone** — when the run should fire
* **What to run** — quality checks only, profiling only, or both

Scheduled runs always use the **latest approved** rule set and currently scan the **full table** (not a sample or increment). Draft sample size does not apply to schedules.

![The schedule editor: an hourly/daily/weekly cadence picker with a time and timezone, a cron option, and Save and Remove schedule buttons](/dqx/img/studio/schedule_light.png)![The schedule editor: an hourly/daily/weekly cadence picker with a time and timezone, a cron option, and Save and Remove schedule buttons](/dqx/img/studio/schedule_dark.png)

#### Runs history[​](#runs-history "Direct link to Runs history")

Every past run shows up in **Runs History**, with its status and how long it took — validation runs and profiling runs alike. Once a run finishes, head to [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md) to check the score and investigate any quality issues.


---

### Uptime health checks

[Beta](/dqx/docs/reference/feature_lifecycle.md#beta "Feature lifecycle: Beta")[Available since DQX v0.17.0](https://github.com/databrickslabs/dqx/releases/tag/v0.17.0 "Available since DQX v0.17.0")

DQX Studio exposes read-only **validation-status endpoints** so an external uptime monitor — Site24x7, Pingdom, Datadog, or any checker that can send an HTTP request with a Databricks OAuth token — can poll a table's data-quality health like a service health check. The contract is deliberately simple:

* **200 OK** — the latest completed run passed (no error rows).
* **503 Service Unavailable** — the run failed, was canceled, found error rows, or is older than the freshness bound you asked for.

Point your monitor at one of the endpoints below and alert on any non-200 response.

#### Check the latest run for a table[​](#check-the-latest-run-for-a-table "Direct link to Check the latest run for a table")

```text
GET /api/v1/monitoring/status/table/{table_fqn}

```

Returns the pass/fail status of the **most recently completed** run for a monitored table. `table_fqn` is the three-level Unity Catalog name, e.g. `main.sales.orders`.

In-progress, canceled, and ad-hoc preview runs are skipped — they say nothing about the table's data — so the endpoint always reflects the last real scheduled or on-demand run.

##### Catch a job that stopped running[​](#catch-a-job-that-stopped-running "Direct link to Catch a job that stopped running")

Add `max_age_minutes` to be told when a table's validation has gone quiet. If the latest completed run finished longer ago than this bound, the endpoint returns **503** with `stale: true` instead of serving a stale "all clear":

```text
GET /api/v1/monitoring/status/table/main.sales.orders?max_age_minutes=90

```

Sizing max_age_minutes

Set it to a little more than the table's schedule interval — e.g. ~90 for an hourly schedule — so a run that simply hasn't fired yet doesn't trip the alert, but a validation job that has actually stopped does. The maximum is 129600 (90 days), which matches the default run-history retention.

#### Check a specific run[​](#check-a-specific-run "Direct link to Check a specific run")

```text
GET /api/v1/monitoring/status/run/{run_id}

```

Returns the status of one run by its id. Unlike the by-table endpoint, a **canceled** run is reported here (as 503) rather than skipped — you asked for that specific run, so its outcome is surfaced. Preview runs are still excluded.

#### Response[​](#response "Direct link to Response")

Both endpoints return the same minimal body:

| Field              | Description                                                       |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `status`           | `SUCCESS`, `FAILED`, or `CANCELED`                                |
| `source_table_fqn` | The table the run validated                                       |
| `run_id`           | The run's id                                                      |
| `error_rows`       | Rows that failed an error-level check (clean when 0 or null)      |
| `warning_rows`     | Rows that failed a warning-level check (do not affect pass/fail)  |
| `updated_at`       | When the run completed                                            |
| `stale`            | `true` when the run is older than the requested `max_age_minutes` |

Other status codes: **404** when no completed run exists for the table (or the run id is unknown), and **400** for a malformed table name or run id.

Warnings don't fail the check

Only error rows drive the 200/503 result. A clean run with warning rows still returns 200 — warnings are reported in the body for context but don't mark the table "down".

#### Authentication[​](#authentication "Direct link to Authentication")

Call the endpoints with a Databricks OAuth token for a principal that has any DQX Studio role (**Viewer** is enough). Most uptime monitors let you set a static `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header:

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DATABRICKS_TOKEN" \
  "https://<app-host>/api/v1/monitoring/status/table/main.sales.orders?max_age_minutes=90"

```

A `200` means the table is healthy and fresh; a `503` means your monitor should raise an alert.


---

### Quickstart: your first monitored table in 10 minutes

This is a start-to-finish walkthrough for someone opening DQX Studio for the first time. By the end you'll have a rule you built, applied to a real table, run, with results on screen — no code.

Follow the steps in order. Each one builds on the last.

Before you start

You'll need a table in Unity Catalog that you already have access to. DQX Studio only ever shows you data you can already see, so pick a table you know — an `orders`, `customers`, or similar table works well.

#### 0. Set up DQX Studio (administrators, once)[​](#0-set-up-dqx-studio-administrators-once "Direct link to 0. Set up DQX Studio (administrators, once)")

[Beta](/dqx/docs/reference/feature_lifecycle.md#beta "Feature lifecycle: Beta")[Available since DQX v0.17.0](https://github.com/databrickslabs/dqx/releases/tag/v0.17.0 "Available since DQX v0.17.0")

If your workspace administrator has already installed Studio and it opens to the home page, skip to step 1. Otherwise an administrator completes this once. The full procedure, including the Declarative Automation Bundle route, is in the [installation guide](/dqx/docs/installation.md#dqx-studio-installation).

Breaking change: fresh installs only

This release changes Studio's storage layout and permission model. There is no upgrade path from earlier installations: remove the previous app, its task-runner job, warehouse, Unity Catalog schemas, and Lakebase project before installing.

1. **Install** DQX Studio from the Databricks Marketplace and bind a SQL warehouse and a Lakebase endpoint.
2. **Share the app** with your audience group and your administrator group (**Compute → Apps → DQX Studio → Permissions → Can Use**).
3. **Open Studio as a workspace administrator** and fill in the setup form: the **catalog**, a **storage prefix** (default `dqx_studio`), and the **audience group** (an existing group such as `dqx-studio-users`).
4. **Run the `GRANT` statements** setup prints, if any, and choose **Verify again** until every step is green. If the app's sharing cannot be verified, setup shows a warning instead; confirm step 2 manually.
5. **Assign roles** in **Admin Settings → Entitlements** so the audience groups become Authors, Approvers, and Viewers.

See [Permissions & Entitlements](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/permissions-and-entitlements.md) for exactly what each group needs.

#### 1. Create a reusable rule[​](#1-create-a-reusable-rule "Direct link to 1. Create a reusable rule")

A **rule** is a reusable definition of a data-quality expectation — for example, "this column is never blank". Author it once here, and you'll be able to apply it to as many tables as you like.

Go to **Rules** and choose **New rule**. You'll fill in two tabs:

* On the **About** tab, give the rule a **name** and a short **description**, pick a **default severity** (**Low**, **Medium**, **High**, or **Critical**), and choose a **dimension** (such as completeness or validity — the quality aspect this rule measures).
* On the **Implementation** tab, pick a check from **Basic Rules** — for example **is not null**, which flags any blank value. That's all a simple rule needs.

![Creating a rule — the Basic Rules check picker showing the built-in check catalog grouped by category with search](/dqx/img/studio/create_rule_basic_checks_light.png)![Creating a rule — the Basic Rules check picker showing the built-in check catalog grouped by category with search](/dqx/img/studio/create_rule_basic_checks_dark.png)

Prefer to describe it in words?

On the About tab you can also describe the rule in plain English and let **AI** generate the check for you. See [Create a rule](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md) for both approaches.

Save the rule. It lands in your **Rules Registry** — your library of reusable rules — ready to apply.

#### 2. Add a table to monitor[​](#2-add-a-table-to-monitor "Direct link to 2. Add a table to monitor")

Before you can apply a rule to a table, you register the table with DQX Studio.

Go to **Tables** and choose **Monitor a table**. Browse Unity Catalog and pick the table you chose above. Because DQX Studio only shows data you already have access to, if a table isn't listed it's a permissions matter, not a bug.

#### 3. Apply your rule to the table[​](#3-apply-your-rule-to-the-table "Direct link to 3. Apply your rule to the table")

Open your table and go to its **Apply Rules** tab. Find the column your rule fits and apply the rule to it. This turns the rule into a **check** — the same rule can become many checks across different columns and tables.

Here you can override the rule's defaults for this table:

* **Severity** — keep the rule's default, or change it for this check. Severity is a priority for triage and reporting; it doesn't decide pass or fail.
* **Pass threshold** — optionally require that, say, "70% of rows must pass" before the check counts as healthy. Thresholds are set per rule and per column, which is handy for gradual clean-up. See [Set quality thresholds](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md#quality-thresholds).

Your table is now a **monitored table** — the single place to see and manage that table's data quality.

#### 4. Let it go through approval[​](#4-let-it-go-through-approval "Direct link to 4. Let it go through approval")

Rules don't go live the instant you make them: your check is submitted for review, and an approver signs off before it becomes active. See the [Approval workflow](/dqx/docs/studio/governance/approval-workflow.md). For this walkthrough, assume it's approved.

#### 5. Run the checks[​](#5-run-the-checks "Direct link to 5. Run the checks")

With an active check in place, trigger a run from your monitored table. DQX Studio reads the table and evaluates the check against every row. It never changes your data; it only reports what it finds. See [Run checks & schedule](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/run-and-schedule.md).

#### 6. See your results[​](#6-see-your-results "Direct link to 6. See your results")

When the run finishes, open the table's **Results**. You'll see an overall **data quality score** and a breakdown of what passed and what didn't. The useful part is the **Failed records** table — hover a failing row to see exactly which checks it failed, each with its severity and the reason, so you know what to fix.

![A Results view — hovering a failing row shows a popup listing the checks it failed with severity and reason](/dqx/img/studio/failed_record_popup_light.png)![A Results view — hovering a failing row shows a popup listing the checks it failed with severity and reason](/dqx/img/studio/failed_record_popup_dark.png)

That's the whole loop: a rule, applied to a table, run, with results you can act on. See [Review results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md) to read a score and work through the rows that didn't pass.

Failing rows are safe to inspect

A failing check never deletes or edits your data. Failing rows are copied into a quarantine table so you can triage them.

#### What next?[​](#what-next "Direct link to What next?")

* **[Key concepts](/dqx/docs/studio.md#key-concepts)** — the handful of ideas (rules vs checks vs tests, the three levels, roles) that make everything else click.
* **[Create a rule](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md)** — go deeper on building rules, including custom conditions and AI generation.
* **[Monitor a table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring.md)** — register more tables and apply your rules across them.


---

### Review results

After a [run](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/run-and-schedule.md) finishes, its results show up here — where you read the quality score, see which checks failed, and drill into the failing rows to decide what to fix. Every monitored table and collection has a **Results** view.

#### Read the score[​](#read-the-score "Direct link to Read the score")

At the top is the **DQ score** — a 0–100% summary of the latest run. A rule becomes a **check** when you apply it to a column, and each check produces one **test** per row when it runs; the score is the **average test pass rate** across all of them. A **collection** score is the average DQ score across its member tables. Below the score, breakdowns split the results by **dimension**, **severity**, **rule**, and **column**, so you can see where quality is slipping.

A check is **flagged as failing** when its pass rate drops below its [pass threshold](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/assign-rules.md#quality-thresholds) (the `< 70%` badge) — that's separate from the numeric score, which always uses the raw pass rate.

#### Investigate and act on a failure[​](#investigate-and-act-on-a-failure "Direct link to Investigate and act on a failure")

The breakdowns are interactive: select a **dimension**, **severity**, **rule**, or **column** to filter down to just those results, and on a collection you can **drill into a member table** to open its own Results and keep going. To see what actually went wrong, open the **Failed records** table and **hover a failing cell** — a popup lists every check that flagged the row, each with its severity and reason.

![Failed records table with a hovered row showing a popup of the checks that row failed, each with severity and reason](/dqx/img/studio/failed_record_popup_light.png)![Failed records table with a hovered row showing a popup of the checks that row failed, each with severity and reason](/dqx/img/studio/failed_record_popup_dark.png)

A failing check is a signal to act, not always a problem with the rule. You can **fix the data at source**, **adjust the threshold** if the target was unrealistic, **change the severity** to reprioritize, **refine the rule**, or **escalate** to the team that owns the data. The **Show comments** control opens a notes thread so you can record what you found and hand it off — each comment keeps its author and timestamp.

Your data is never changed

Failing a check never deletes or edits your data. The failing rows shown here are copied into a quarantine table purely so you can inspect them — you can also [query that table directly](#analyse-in-lakehouse).

#### Ask Genie[​](#ask-genie "Direct link to Ask Genie")

**Ask Genie** turns your results into a conversation. Open the panel on any Results view and ask a question in plain English — "which columns have the most failures?", "why did my score drop?" — and Genie answers with a short explanation and, where it helps, a chart. There's no SQL to write; it's built on Databricks Genie and reads the same results you're already looking at.

Not sure what to ask? Genie opens with **suggested questions** grouped by what you're trying to do — Basic stats, Drilldown, Trends over time, and Diagnose. Every conversation stays with the table or collection you opened it from, and you can start a **New conversation** or revisit an earlier one from **History** at any time.

#### Analyse in Lakehouse[​](#analyse-in-lakehouse "Direct link to Analyse in Lakehouse")

Failing rows captured by Studio's runs land in a Delta table in your Studio catalog, which you can query outside the app from SQL, a notebook, or an alerting job:

```sql
SELECT quarantine_id, run_id, created_at, row_data, errors, warnings
FROM <catalog>.<prefix>.dq_quarantine_records  -- default prefix: dqx_studio
WHERE source_table_fqn = 'main.sales.orders'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

```

`row_data` holds the full source row and `errors` / `warnings` the checks it failed, all as [`VARIANT`](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/semi-structured/variant). Because the rows are real source data, treat the table as a possible PII surface and grant access accordingly. Records are deleted after `quarantine_retention_days` (default 30).

The table may not hold **every** failing row: draft runs evaluate only a sample of the source table, and cross-table SQL checks cap their quarantine at 100,000 rows. Row-level checks on a full or scheduled run write the complete invalid set. Keep that in mind when building alerting or triage jobs on it.

For more recipes — reading fields out of the source row, exploding failed checks into rows, counting failures by check, and joining to run details — see the [Query Results Cookbook](/dqx/docs/reference/query_results_cookbook.md#dqx-studio-quarantine-records).


---

### Theme

[Beta](/dqx/docs/reference/feature_lifecycle.md#beta "Feature lifecycle: Beta")[Available since DQX v0.17.0](https://github.com/databrickslabs/dqx/releases/tag/v0.17.0 "Available since DQX v0.17.0")

Admins can brand DQX Studio for their company under **Settings → Theme**. It applies to every Studio user. Users still choose light or dark mode themselves.

#### Branding[​](#branding "Direct link to Branding")

* **Company name** adds your company to the top bar: **DQX Studio | Acme**. It saves as you type. Reset it to show **DQX Studio** only.
* **Logo** replaces the DQX icon in the top bar. Click a logo preview, or drop an image onto it, to upload. The previews show the logo on the light and dark mode top bars. Your first logo is used in both modes; after that, uploading to the light or dark preview changes only that mode.
* Logos must be PNG, JPEG or WebP, up to 256 KB. SVG isn't supported. Logos are shown 24 px tall and up to 160 px wide, so a logo about 200 px tall is plenty.

#### Theme[​](#theme-1 "Direct link to Theme")

Pick a preset or set five colours: **Brand** (top bar), **Sidebar**, **Page background**, **Interactive elements** (buttons and highlights) and **Text**. Studio derives the rest (cards, hover, borders, button text) from them.

* Use **Light** and **Dark** next to **Colours** to choose which mode's colours you are editing. The preview always shows both modes.
* Changing a colour in one mode generates the same colour in the other mode, until you set that one yourself.
* Saving changes updates the selected preset, built-in or custom. **Reset theme** restores a built-in preset's original colours.
* **Add new** starts a theme with no colours set. As you fill in colours, the same colours in the other mode are generated for you. Saving it adds **Custom 1**, **Custom 2** and so on. Click a custom theme's name to rename it, or delete it with its bin icon.
* If a colour combination may be hard to read, Studio shows a warning that names the colour to adjust. You can still save.
* Status colours (pass, warn, fail) and chart colours don't change.
* **Reset theme** restores the original colours of the preset you started from. It doesn't change the company name, logo or custom presets, and isn't shown for custom presets.

Presets: DQX Studio (the default), Databricks, High contrast, Aubergine, Dracula, Nord, Ocean and Solarized.

Execution Environment

When DQX is installed in the workspace as a tool, it provides a suite of command-line tools for executing DQX jobs (see the [User Guide](/dqx/docs/guide.md)).

#### DQX Studio[​](#dqx-studio "Direct link to DQX Studio")

If you're using [DQX Studio](/dqx/docs/studio.md), the no-code web app, you can try the **app built-in demo** so you can explore every feature against realistic data before pointing it at your own tables. It creates a small set of sample tables, a library of reusable rules, monitored tables, collections, and past runs — enough to see scores, trends, failing records, and the approval workflow in action.

An admin deploys the demo from the [Rule Marketplace](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/rule-marketplace.md) — it's the **Deploy demo content** action at the top of the page. Deploying it sets up the sample catalog, seeds the rules and monitored tables, and generates a history of runs so the results views have something to show. Once it's in place you can:

* Browse the [rules registry](/dqx/docs/studio/authoring/create-a-rule.md) and see how rules are reused across tables.
* Open a [monitored table](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring.md) and [review its results](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md) — including failing records you can inspect.
* View a [collection](/dqx/docs/studio/monitoring/collections.md) such as *Customer 360* to see quality across related tables at once.
* Try [Ask Genie](/dqx/docs/studio/running.md#ask-genie) on the demo's results.

It's the fastest way for a new steward or reviewer to get comfortable — nothing they do to the demo touches production data.
